This page explains how releases are cut and versioned across the Deploy App repos, where to read release notes, and how to pin a reproducible legacy deployment. Versioning tooling conventions are summarized on Community & Standards; this page is about the release artifacts and compatibility.

The on-site Releases feed

This documentation site carries a Releases feed so you can see what changed without leaving the docs.

Where release notes live (per component)

Release-note conventions differ by repo:

  • **docker-rasenmaeher-integration** (legacy stack) keeps human-written notes in-repo under docs/releases/*.md, one file per version (e.g. 2.7.1.md, 2.8.0.md). Each note follows a consistent template: TL;DR, Release Goals, New mandatory ENV variables, New features, Improvements & fixes, Breaking changes, Security, Other changes, and Contributors — with links to the PRs/commits in each affected submodule. These are the authoritative upgrade notes for the stack; read the relevant version's note (especially "New mandatory ENV variables" and "Breaking changes") before pulling a new tag.
  • Product integrations and other components version per repo with bump-my-version and publish notes via GitHub Releases tied to their tags. CI enforces a bump on every PR via the shared validate-bumpversion action.

Version scheme

  • The legacy stack uses a single integration version (e.g. 2.8.0) recorded in version.yml; a CI job parses that file and creates the matching git tag on push to main.

  • Product integrations use semver-ish strings, often with a date build suffix — for example matrix-rmapi 1.1.1+260512, and the template seeds 0.0.1+<yymmdd>. Bump with:

    bump-my-version bump <patch|minor|major>
bump-my-version show-bump   # preview what each option would do

Pinning a reproducible legacy deployment

The legacy stack is the canonical example of "pin a consistent set." Because its components are submodules at specific commits, always deploy from a tag so the submodule combination is the tested one:

git tag                                   # list available tags
git checkout <TAG_NAME>                    # choose a specific tag
git submodule update --init --recursive   # move submodules to that tag's commits
docker compose build                       # build the matched set
Updating to a newer release is the same idea — pull, re-sync submodules, then pull/build images:

git pull
git submodule update --init --recursive
docker compose pull
docker compose up -d

Do not run individual submodules at arbitrary commits in production; the tag is what guarantees the combination has been tested together.

Image tags

CI publishes container images via the shared publish-image action to the configured registries (GHCR / Docker Hub / ACR). The legacy compose files reference images through PVARKI_DOCKER_REPO and a release tag (the integration template's generated service line uses an image tag derived from RELEASE_TAG), so the image set tracks the integration release tag.

Core vs integration compatibility

Product integrations are driven by the core rmapi over mTLS user-lifecycle callbacks (created / revoked / promoted / demoted / updated). Compatibility is therefore defined by that callback contract and the kraftwerk manifest the core provides, not by matching version numbers. Practical guidance:

  • An integration must implement the callback surface the core version expects; when the core changes that contract, integrations follow.
  • In the legacy stack, the tested combination is the one captured by the integration tag and its submodule pointers — that is your compatibility guarantee. When adding a new integration, you bump MW_PRODUCTS and wire it into the composition (see Build an Integration), then the whole set is re-tagged.
  • Read the legacy release note's "New mandatory ENV variables" and "Breaking changes" sections before upgrading, since a new integration often adds required secrets (e.g. 2.8.0 added the SYNAPSE_* and RMMTX_SRT_* variables when Matrix landed).
